## Block A — Why bioengineering needs computation

**Reductionism vs. systems biology.** Molecular biology takes a system apart
and understands one module very well — powerful, and the source of almost
everything we know. Systems biology puts the modules back together and
studies their interactions: a metabolic network is not a list of enzymes, it
is a web of couplings between them. The engineering consequence: to change
what a cell makes, you have to reason about the whole network, not one gene.

**The Ship of Theseus.** If every molecule in a cell is replaced over time, is
it still the same cell? What persists is the *pattern of interactions*, not
the stuff — and that pattern is what a model tries to capture (Kacser, 1957:
"the properties of a system are in fact more than the sum of the properties
of its components").

**Where the numbers come from.** Omics data (genomics, transcriptomics,
proteomics, metabolomics, fluxomics), high-throughput tech (NGS, LC/MS,
robotic screening, automated cultivation — you'll meet the automation side in
meetings 7–8 with Pioreactor), and biological databases (NCBI, UniProt, KEGG,
MetaCyc, BiGG Models, BioModels). A model is only as good as the measurements
behind it, and the bookkeeping that keeps those measurements findable.

**Genome annotation vs. network annotation.** Genome annotation answers "what
genetic material is present?" and produces a catalogue. Network annotation
answers "what biochemical activity is possible?" and produces a *computable
model*. Turning the first into the second is called reconstruction — the
subject of meetings 4–6. A genome-scale metabolic model (GSMM) is a computable
inventory of every reaction an organism can catalyse (typically 1 000–10 000
reactions). It needs no kinetic constants, which is exactly why it scales to
a whole organism, unlike the kinetic models built next week. Two companies
that build GSMMs for a living: Novo Nordisk (via the Novo Nordisk Foundation,
which funds DTU Biosustain, co-developers of COBRApy — used in meeting 4) and
Novonesis.

## Block B — From networks to dynamics

A network diagram (nodes = things whose amounts change; links = the processes
that change them) tells you what is *possible* — topology, motifs, hubs. Only
a dynamic model tells you what actually *happens*: oscillation, bistability,
adaptation. Three ways to turn a network into a model, in increasing realism
(and required data): topology only → a stoichiometric matrix (meetings 4–6) →
rate laws + parameters (meetings 2–3). More mechanism means more realism, and
far more parameters to measure — that trade-off never goes away.

**State variables** are what the system *is* right now (concentration,
population, membrane potential) — what the ODE solves for. **Parameters** are
what the system's *rules* are (rate constants, half-saturation, maximum
rate) — fixed during a run. In the game: state variables are how many candies
and sticky notes are on the grid; parameters are the rules on the rules card.

A first-order ODE, `dx/dt = f(x)`, says: give me the state now, and the rule
`f` tells me where it goes next — which is also a description of the game.
Three named models to know:

- **Linear birth–degradation** — steady state depends on the degradation
  rate; half-life `t½ = ln 2 / k_deg`. Biological analogy: an mRNA
  transcribed at a constant rate and degraded by RNases.
- **Logistic growth** — steady states at `N = 0` (unstable) and `N = K`
  (stable); growth is fast when `N ≪ K` and stalls as `N → K`. Analogy: a
  bacterial culture in a flask. Today's grassland has exactly 36 cells — that
  is `K`.
- **Lotka–Volterra predator–prey** — `+αR` (prey breed), `−βRF` (prey die on
  encounter), `+δRF` (predators breed from what they catch), `−γF`
  (predators starve without prey). Today's model.

When `solve_ivp(...)` draws a curve, it did not solve the equation on paper —
it started from the given state, applied the rule to get the change over a
small step, updated the state, and repeated, thousands of times. For the next
45 minutes there are no computers: you are the processor, the candies are the
state, and the rules card is the model.

## Block C — The Rabbit & Fox game

45 minutes, no computers. Candies are rabbits, sticky notes are foxes, and
you are the numerical solver. (Adapted from the MnSTEP predator–prey
activity, SERC, Carleton College.)

**Per group of four:** a 6×6 grid (≈50×50 cm), 40 candies (rabbits), 12
sticky notes (foxes, each covering a 2×2 patch), one tally sheet. One person
scatters, one drops, one counts, one records — rotate every round. At most
one candy per cell.

**Version 1.** Start: 4 rabbits, 1 fox. Each generation: scatter the
surviving rabbits at random, drop each fox's note (order matters — foxes are
resolved one at a time), remove every rabbit caught, a fox that caught ≥3
survives (otherwise it starves), every survivor doubles for the next
generation. *What usually happens:* with only 4 rabbits on 36 cells, a fox
almost never finds 3 in one patch — it starves immediately and nothing brings
it back. Rabbits then double until the grid is full and stay there. Two
state variables, one stuck at zero. Why: the meadow was sealed (nothing lets
animals wander in), flat (no refuge anywhere), and extinction was absorbing
(no way back from zero). A model fails when it leaves out a process that
matters.

**Version 2 — immigration.** If foxes hit 0 at the end of a turn, 1 fox
wanders in; if rabbits hit 0, 3 rabbits wander in. Everything else unchanged.
This is a constant supply from outside the system boundary — a `+k` term
that doesn't depend on the state, and it's exactly what makes a system *open*
rather than closed (Meeting 2).

**Version 3 — a sanctuary.** Keep version 2's rule, and mark a 2×2 corner
where rabbits may sit but foxes may not hunt. An 11%-of-the-grid refuge does
not change the outcome by 11% — it changes the *kind* of behaviour: without
one, prey/predator booms and crashes risk hitting zero forever; with one, a
guaranteed floor of prey puts a floor under the predators' food supply, and
the swings damp instead of crashing. (The same structure reappears in
metabolic engineering as a bypass route guaranteeing a minimum flux to an
essential pathway.)

**Translating the game into the equation you'll meet next week:**

| What you did on the grid | The term | Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| Surviving rabbits double | `+αR` | α ≈ 0.7 / generation |
| A fox's note lands on rabbits | `−βRF` | β = chance of overlap |
| A fox with ≥3 catches breeds | `+δRF` | δ = conversion efficiency |
| A fox with <3 catches starves | `−γF` | γ = starvation rate |
| The grid holds only 36 candies | `× (1 − R/K)` | K = 36 |
| Animals wander in | `+k` (constant influx) | k = 1 fox, 3 rabbits |
| The sanctuary corner | predation acts on `(R − R_safe)` | R_safe |

Your game is Euler's method with `Δt` = one generation — the crudest possible
solver. Too large a step doesn't just blur the answer; it can manufacture
behaviour the model doesn't actually contain (you'll see this on screen next
week). And every group, playing identical rules, got a different graph — not
experimental error, but a property of the system when numbers are small and
chance (where the note lands) is built in.

## Block D — Your working environment

**Reproducibility is the rule of the practicum.** A result you cannot re-run
is not a result, it's an anecdote. In practice: every number in your report
traces to a notebook cell, every notebook runs top to bottom on a fresh
runtime with no manual steps, every input file is named for what it is and
lives somewhere findable.

**The toolchain** (all open source, runs in a browser, nothing to install
today):

| Tool | What it is | From meeting |
|---|---|---|
| Google Colab | A Jupyter notebook on Google's machines, in your browser | 1 |
| Python + NumPy | The language and its array maths | 2 |
| SciPy (`solve_ivp`) | Numerical integration of ODEs | 2 |
| Matplotlib | Plots | 2 |
| COBRApy | Constraint-based analysis of genome-scale models | 4 |
| Escher | Interactive metabolic pathway maps | 5 |
| Pioreactor | An open-source bench-top bioreactor | 7 |

**A computational notebook** holds three things at once: the code that
produced a result, the result itself, and your narrative for why. The
classic failure is cells run out of order, which only works on your screen —
the cure, and the test applied to every notebook you hand in, is *Runtime →
Restart and run all* before you submit.

**Data management:** one folder per student in Google Drive,
`BIMB265125_<yourname>/M01_intro/{raw,notebooks,figures}` and so on per
meeting, with a `journal.md`. `raw/` is read-only — write a new file if data
must change. Name files so alphabetical sort is also sensible sort (e.g.
`M02_fig01_closed_system.png`); no spaces, no `final_final_v3`.
